maincpu.name: Foreground videoram
maincpu.notes: code low byte at tile_index, code hi bit + unused at 0x400+tile_index

maincpu.name: Background videoram
maincpu.notes: two selectable 0x400 pages (video_control bit2), code hi bit at page|0x200|tile_index

maincpu.name: Video control register
maincpu.notes: D0-1 fg text color, D2 bg page select, D4-5 coin counters, D7 screen flip; shared as video_control

maincpu.name: Background Y scroll register
maincpu.notes: write-only, shared as scroll; applied via tilemap set_scrolly

maincpu.name: AY8910 shared data latch
maincpu.notes: write-only, shared as ay8910_data; combined with select latch at 0x2040 to emulate discrete BDIR/BC1 bus

maincpu.name: AY8910 BDIR/BC1 select latch
maincpu.notes: bit5/4 -> ay1 BDIR/BC1 edge, bit7/6 -> ay2 BDIR/BC1 edge; no read handler (nopr)

maincpu.name: Unused I/O slot
maincpu.notes: no read or write handler installed (noprw)

maincpu.name: Palette RAM
maincpu.notes: 32 bytes, low half of the 64-entry palette (mirror mask 0x1f80)

layers.name: sprites
layers.notes: gfx region fgtiles_sprites decoded with 16x16 3bpp planar layout, palette base 0, 2 color groups (16 colors); code = (attr bit4<<4)|spriteram[+1], flip bits in attr

layers.name: fg (text)
layers.notes: transparent pen 0, palette base 32, color from video_control bits 0-1, TILEMAP_SCAN_COLS_FLIP_X

layers.name: bg (scroll)
layers.notes: palette base 16, 1 color group; two selectable ROM pages via video_control bit2; per-row Y flip when (tile_index & 0x10)

palette.notes: Low 32 entries (index bit5=0) are RAM-backed (paletteram, CPU writable); high 32 entries (index bit5=1) are hardwired from the 32-byte color PROM (ic61/hlo/82s123). Both halves feed the same 3-3-2 resistor-weighted RGB DAC (R/G taps 4.7k/3.3k/1.5k, B taps 3.3k/1.5k).

custom_chips: HMC20 (video timing/sync generator, inferred from driver comment - not confirmed by schematic text)
video.dac_type: Resistor ladder (weighted-resistor network), not a dedicated DAC IC — consistent with pcb.notes stating no custom video silicon was identified, only discrete TTL plus the color PROM
video.sync_generation: board_spec attributes video timing/sync to a chip labeled 'HMC20' from a driver source comment, but flags it as unconfirmed by schematic text; the schematic PDF available for this run is scanned with no OCR layer, so this could not be verified or contradicted
video.layer_priority_logic: confidence: low — not independently derivable from the available (scanned, textless) schematic; board_spec's video_control register bits (fg text color, bg page select) suggest priority is likely register/CPU-controlled rather than a dedicated priority PROM, but no PROM beyond the 32-byte color PROM (ic61/82s123) appears in the ROM listing to support a hardware priority-encoder theory

audio.mixing: mono - both AY8910s summed to a single speaker channel at 0.30 gain each; the two chips share one 8-bit data bus (0x2030) and are addressed by toggling a select latch (0x2040) that emulates each chip's discrete BDIR/BC1 pins

mame.history:
Arcade Video game published 42 years ago:

Mysterious Stones (c) 1984 Technos Japan Corp.

- TECHNICAL -

Game ID : TA-0010

Main CPU : MOS Technology M6502 (@ 1.5 Mhz)
Sound Chips : (2x) General Instrument AY8910 (@ 1.5 Mhz)

Players : 2
Control : 4-way joystick
Buttons : 2

- TRIVIA -

Mysterious Stones was released in November 1984.

With this game, Technos Japan developers pushed even further the peculiar gameplay elements on which "Eggs" and "Scrambled Egg" were based, by putting them into an Indy-themed, multi-room mayhem.

- UPDATES -

The subtitle is slightly different between the new and old versions. The new version says 'Dr. John's Adventure' while the old version says 'Dr. Kick In Adventure'.

- TIPS AND TRICKS -

By hitting the lonely idol statue in the opening screen with a headbonk, a secret message will be displayed: 'A short cut to a treasure room. Go into an upper or a lower entrance. And... Go on left!'. This obviously refers to the game map. As a side note, the older version of the game displays the same message in Japanese katakana characters, an eloquent proof that the older Mysterious Stones set was meant for use in Japan only.

- CONTRIBUTE -

Edit this entry: https://www.arcade-history.com/game/1714/?o=2

pcb.notes: No custom silicon identified; discrete TTL logic plus a 32-byte color PROM. Schematics.pdf reference exists but is a scanned image with no extractable text.

jtframe_hints.recommended_template: No existing JTframe core matches this early discrete-logic Technos hardware closely enough to use as a template; build from the base jtframe scaffold using a generic 6502 + raster video pipeline.
jtframe_hints.reference_jtcore: jt49 (AY-3-8910) for both sound chips; no CPU-core match in the current public registry

sdram_layout.bank0: maincpu program ROM (0x4000-0xffff region, 0x10000 total, only upper 48KB populated)
sdram_layout.bank1: fgtiles_sprites graphics ROM (0xc000, 3bpp planar, shared by fg tilemap and sprite layer)
sdram_layout.bank2: bgtiles graphics ROM (0xc000, 3bpp planar, background tilemap)
sdram_layout.bank3: unused — color PROM (0x20 bytes) is small enough to load into BRAM instead of SDRAM

jtframe_hints.ioctl_notes: Color PROM (32B) and palette RAM (32B) are tiny — keep the whole 64-entry palette in BRAM/LUTs rather than SDRAM. No NVRAM/EEPROM in this design (no battery-backed high scores). DIP switches map straight to core status bits.
jtframe_hints.clock_requirements: Single 12MHz master XTAL; CPU (M6502) and both AY8910s run at master/8 = 1.5MHz; pixel clock is master/2 = 6MHz driving the 384x272 total raster (256x240 visible, 57.44Hz refresh).
special_considerations: No M6502 CPU core is present in the public JTframe module registry (fx68k, jtkcpu, HUC6280, jtdsp16, jt680x listed) — an external 6502-compatible core (e.g. T65) must be sourced separately.

Both AY8910s share a single 8-bit data bus (0x2030) and are selected via a latch (0x2040) that emulates discrete BDIR/BC1 pin toggling on each chip — implement as a small edge-detect FSM rather than simple chip-select decoding.
Palette is split: low 32 entries are CPU-writable RAM, high 32 entries are hardwired from the color PROM; both halves feed the same 3-3-2 resistor-weighted RGB DAC.

Background tilemap selects between two ROM-backed pages via video_control bit 2, and applies per-row Y flip based on tile_index bit 4 — an unusual per-row flip baked into the tile decode rather than a global flag.
Screen flip (video_control bit 7) is XORed against a DIP switch bit (DSW1 bit 5) rather than driven by either source alone — cocktail flip logic must combine both.

Interrupts are a software-timed 16-per-frame scanline chain (starting at line 8, spaced every 16 lines, cleared via a write to 0x2010) rather than a single vblank IRQ — the FPGA timing generator needs to reproduce this cadence, not just pulse once per frame.

_enrichment_summary: Very little could be confidently added beyond what MAME Scout already extracted for this board. The only PCB documentation available (Mysterious Stones Schematics.pdf) is a scanned image with no text layer, so it could not be parsed for register maps, pinouts, or component values. The supplied 'Hardware Reference' material is the generic MAME netlist engine changelog (audio/nl_konami.cpp, solver internals, etc.) and does not reference Technos, the TA-0010 board, or any AY8910/discrete-logic circuitry used by this game — mystston's audio path is driven directly by two AY8910 PSGs via MAME's ay8910 device, not the netlist analog solver, so none of that changelog is applicable here. Enrichment below is limited to restructuring/clarifying facts already implicit in board_spec.json (clock fan-out, DAC topology) without introducing new unverified data. No custom ICs are enriched because board_spec.custom_ics is empty and no schematic text was available to identify any.
